text: In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index, and every secondary-index record also stores the primary-key columns. A long key therefore also bloats the expired_at index: MySQL notes 'it is advantageous to have a short primary key'.
why: Shows a second, non-obvious cost of the key size choice.

text: MySQL BLOB size classes: TINYBLOB < 256 B, BLOB < 64 KB, MEDIUMBLOB < 16 MB, LONGBLOB < 4 GB. A value column meant to hold multi-megabyte objects must be MEDIUMBLOB or LONGBLOB.
why: The lecture's 10 MB value example would not fit a plain BLOB.

text: PostgreSQL upsert syntax: INSERT INTO store (key, value, expired_at) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value, expired_at = EXCLUDED.expired_at; EXCLUDED refers to the row that was proposed for insertion.
why: Gives the working statement the lecture's 'UPSERT' stands for.

text: MySQL REPLACE INTO deletes the existing row and inserts a new one ('It either inserts, or deletes and inserts'). INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE modifies the existing row in place. For a put that replaces a value, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE avoids the extra delete.
why: Readers otherwise assume REPLACE is a cheap update.

text: Get-then-insert is also racy: two concurrent puts can both see 'key absent' and one INSERT then fails on the primary key. PostgreSQL documents that ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE yields an atomic insert-or-update outcome 'even under high concurrency'.
why: Adds the correctness argument for upsert, not just the performance one.

text: Redis uses the same idea: 'Keys expiring information is stored as absolute Unix timestamps (in milliseconds in case of Redis version 2.6 or greater)'. Because of that, expiry depends on a stable system clock.
why: Confirms the expired_at design matches how a real KV store does it.

text: For a large backlog, run the cleanup in chunks: MySQL's DELETE ... LIMIT row_count caps rows per statement, and you repeat the DELETE until fewer rows than the limit are affected. That keeps each statement short.
why: Prevents one giant cleanup statement from holding locks for a long time.

text: If 'no TTL' is stored as NULL, comparisons like ttl > NOW() return NULL, so such rows never match. Use a far-future sentinel for 'no expiry', or write (ttl IS NULL OR ttl > NOW()) in GET and the user-delete UPDATE.
why: Plugs a bug readers will hit when implementing the exercise.

text: MySQL TIMESTAMP only covers '1970-01-01 00:00:01' to '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC. For an expiry column use DATETIME (to 9999-12-31) or an integer epoch, which also allows a -1 marker.
why: Avoids a 2038 problem and explains which column type supports the delete marker.

text: InnoDB does not physically remove a deleted row at once: it is removed by a background purge after it is no longer needed for MVCC or rollback. Index pages are merged only when they fall below MERGE_THRESHOLD (default 50% full).
why: Gives the real mechanics behind 'deletes cause rebalancing'.

text: Redis 6.0 rewrote the active expire cycle and made it tunable: active-expire-effort (1-10, default 1) trades CPU for fewer leftover expired keys. At the default, Redis tries to keep under about 10% of expired keys in memory.
why: Updates the classic 20-keys/25% description to current Redis.

text: Deleting a big key with DEL blocks Redis's main thread, 'even seconds' for large objects. UNLINK removes the key at once and frees its memory on a background thread. The lazyfree-lazy-* options apply the same to eviction, expiry and DEL.
why: Practical consequence of single-threaded command execution.

text: RFC 6455 has Ping and Pong control frames. 'A Ping frame may serve either as a keepalive or as a means to verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive', and the peer must answer with a Pong.
why: Shows how liveness is detected over a WebSocket without HTTP heartbeats.

text: MySQL JSON columns are not indexed directly. To query a field inside the JSON fast, index a generated column that extracts it; InnoDB also supports multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays.
why: Completes the 'query inside the value' option.

text: Both MySQL ('Replication is asynchronous by default') and PostgreSQL streaming replication are asynchronous by default. That small delay is what makes replica reads possibly stale; both offer synchronous or semi-synchronous modes at a latency cost.
why: Grounds the staleness claim in the default configuration.

text: Cross-partition ACID is possible but costs more: DynamoDB's TransactWriteItems commits up to 100 items all-or-nothing, but performs two underlying writes per item (prepare and commit) and cancels on conflicts.
why: Shows the trade-off concretely instead of an absolute 'cannot'.

text: Ignite's link to relational databases is optional external storage: it can act as a caching layer over an RDBMS via CacheStore implementations such as CacheJdbcPojoStore, with read-through on cache misses and write-through on updates.
why: Explains the likely source of the 'built on a relational DB' description.

text: MySQL warns that SKIP LOCKED returns an inconsistent view and is 'not suitable for general transactional work'; it fits queue-like tables. NOWAIT instead fails immediately with an error when the row is locked.
why: Helps readers pick the right lock option for puts.

text: In MySQL, growing a VARCHAR can be done in place only while the length prefix stays the same size (0-255 bytes, or 256+ bytes). Crossing 255 bytes, or changing the data type, needs a full table copy.
why: Makes 'you cannot change it' concrete: which changes are cheap and which rebuild the table.

text: Go goroutines start with small stacks that grow as needed, and the runtime multiplexes them onto multiple OS threads, so a goroutine blocked on I/O does not stall the others.
why: Corrects the 'thread in its own space' picture.
